title: Local anaesthesia
blurb: Infiltrations, blocks and intraligamentary injections, the common agents, cartridge checks, needle safety, aftercare and warning signs.
question: The dentist asks you to set up for an inferior dental block before a lower molar filling. The patient has a heart condition and the dentist asks for 'a cartridge without adrenaline'. Afterwards, the patient asks how long they'll be numb and whether they can grab a hot coffee. What do you prepare, check and tell them?

teach.body: A local anaesthetic (LA) temporarily stops nerves in one area from carrying pain signals, so treatment can be done with the patient awake. The dentist prescribes and gives the injection; dental nurses don't administer LA. Your role is to prepare and check the cartridge and syringe as instructed, pass it safely, reassure and watch the patient, record what was used and give aftercare advice. LA cartridges are prescription-only medicines.

children.label: Topical
children.sub: Gel on mucosa before the needle

rows.label: Injected
values: Into the sulcus near the root apex
Inside the ramus, near the nerve

rows.label: Works because
values: Bone here is thin and porous

rows.label: Numbs
values: One or two teeth and gum
Lower teeth to midline, lip, chin

teach.caption: The lower jaw's thick outer bone in the molar region stops infiltrations working well, so a block is used. It usually numbs half the tongue too, via the lingual nerve.

head: Agent
Vasoconstrictor
Notes
rows: When adrenaline is to be avoided; not in pregnancy
teach.caption: Adrenaline and felypressin are vasoconstrictors: they narrow blood vessels so the LA lasts longer, there is less bleeding, and less drug reaches the bloodstream.

items: Right agent: exactly the one the dentist has asked for.
Intact: no cracks, and the blister pack sealed.
Clear: the solution is not cloudy or discoloured.
Bung: not pushed out beyond the rim, and no large bubble (both suggest freezing or damage).
Record afterwards: agent, number of cartridges, injection type and, in many practices, the batch number.

teach.caption: Needlestick injuries often happen when a needle is resheathed by hand or left exposed on a tray. Follow the sharps injury protocol if one happens.

teach.h: Aftercare: what to tell the patient
teach.body: How long numbness lasts varies with the agent and the injection, so give a rough guide: soft tissues usually stay numb for a few hours, longer after a block. Until feeling returns, avoid eating and hot drinks: the patient can bite their lip, cheek or tongue or burn themselves without noticing. Warn parents to watch children, who often chew a numb lip. Contact the practice if numbness lasts much longer than expected.

teach.h: LA toxicity: signs that get worse

steps.label: Early
steps.sub: Light-headed, tingling around the mouth, ringing in the ears

steps.label: Heart
steps.sub: Low blood pressure, slow or irregular pulse, arrest

teach.caption: Toxicity comes from too much LA or an injection into a blood vessel (why aspirating syringes are used). Stop, call for help, ABCDE, oxygen, dial 999. Fainting is far more common than toxicity.

teach.text: Prilocaine with FELYPRESSIN is the choice when adrenaline should be avoided, but felypressin is avoided in pregnancy. And don't confuse an expected numb lip after an inferior dental block with toxicity: toxicity shows as whole-body signs such as dizziness, slurred speech and twitching.

items: Types: topical, infiltration (upper teeth, lower front), inferior dental block (lower molars), intraligamentary (single tooth).
Agents: lidocaine 2% + adrenaline, articaine 4% + adrenaline, prilocaine 3% + felypressin, mepivacaine 3% plain.
Check agent, expiry, cracks, clarity, bung. Record what was given.
Never resheath by hand; the user disposes into a yellow-lidded sharps bin.
Aftercare: no eating or hot drinks until feeling returns. Know the toxicity signs.

summary: You can now tell an infiltration from a block or intraligamentary injection, match the common agents to their vasoconstrictors and uses, check a cartridge, handle needles safely, give accurate aftercare, and recognise the warning signs of LA toxicity.

A.q: A patient asks how long the numbness from their injection will last. What is the best response?
options: Exactly thirty minutes for every patient
It varies, so give them a rough guide
It will last until the next morning
It wears off as soon as they leave
A.why: Duration depends on the agent and type of injection, so give a rough guide (usually a few hours for soft tissues) rather than a fixed time.

whyNot.0: There is no single fixed duration; it varies with agent and technique.
whyNot.2: Normal LA doesn't last overnight; numbness that long should be reported.
whyNot.3: Numbness persists for some time after treatment, which is why aftercare advice matters.

A.q: While checking an LA cartridge, which finding means you must NOT use it?
options: It is still in its sealed blister pack
The solution is clear and colourless
The bung is pushed out beyond the rim
The expiry date is next year
A.why: An extruded bung suggests the cartridge has been frozen or damaged, so it must be discarded.

whyNot.0: A sealed blister pack is what you want to see.
whyNot.1: A clear, colourless solution is normal.
whyNot.3: An expiry date in the future means it is in date.

A.q: The dentist wants to avoid adrenaline for a patient. Which cartridge are they most likely to ask for?
options: Lidocaine 2% with adrenaline
Articaine 4% with adrenaline 1:100,000
Benzocaine 20% topical gel
Prilocaine 3% with felypressin
A.why: Prilocaine with felypressin contains a different vasoconstrictor and is used when adrenaline is to be avoided.

whyNot.2: Topical gel only numbs the surface; it isn't an injection.

B.q: A patient asks why they should wait before eating until the numbness has gone. What is the best explanation?
options: Food will wash the anaesthetic away
They may bite their lip without feeling it
Chewing makes the anaesthetic last longer
Eating will cause the filling to discolour
B.why: Without feeling, patients can bite their lip, cheek or tongue, or burn themselves with hot drinks, without noticing.

whyNot.0: The anaesthetic is in the tissues, not on the surface; food doesn't wash it away.
whyNot.2: Chewing doesn't change how long LA lasts.
whyNot.3: Discolouration isn't the reason for the advice.

B.q: The dentist is about to fill a lower first molar. Which injection is most likely?
options: Inferior dental block
Palatal infiltration
Buccal infiltration of an upper tooth
Topical anaesthetic only
B.why: Thick bone around lower molars stops infiltrations working reliably, so an inferior dental block numbs the nerve supplying all the lower teeth on that side.

whyNot.1: Palatal injections are for upper teeth.
whyNot.2: This would numb an upper tooth, not a lower molar.
whyNot.3: Topical gel only numbs the surface mucosa.

B.q: After the injection, who should dispose of the used needle, and where?
options: The nurse, after resheathing it carefully by hand
Anyone, into the clinical waste bag
The dentist who used it, into a sharps bin
The nurse, into the amalgam waste pot
B.why: The person who used the sharp is responsible for disposing of it, into a sharps bin (yellow-lidded for used LA needles and cartridges).

whyNot.0: Resheathing by hand is a major cause of needlestick injuries.
whyNot.1: Sharps never go in waste bags; they could injure someone.
whyNot.3: Amalgam waste is a separate stream for amalgam only.

C.q: Shortly after an injection, the patient says they feel light-headed and their ears are ringing, then their speech slurs. What might this suggest?
options: Normal soft tissue numbness
Possible LA toxicity
An allergy to latex gloves
A successful block
C.why: Light-headedness, tinnitus and slurred speech are early signs of LA toxicity. Stop, call for help and follow ABCDE.

whyNot.0: Normal numbness is local: lip, tongue and gum, not ringing ears or slurred speech.
whyNot.2: Latex allergy shows as itching, rash, swelling or wheeze, not ringing ears.
whyNot.3: A successful block numbs the lip and tongue; it doesn't affect hearing or speech.

C.q: Why is adrenaline added to many LA cartridges?
options: To raise the patient's blood pressure
To speed up the patient's heart rate and output
To prolong numbness and reduce bleeding
To make the solution taste better
C.why: Adrenaline narrows blood vessels, keeping the LA in place for longer, reducing bleeding and slowing absorption into the blood.

whyNot.0: Raising blood pressure is an unwanted effect, not the purpose.
whyNot.1: A faster heart rate can happen but is a side effect, not the aim.
whyNot.3: Taste isn't the reason; the solution is injected.

C.q: The dentist plans an intraligamentary injection. Where is the anaesthetic deposited?
options: Around the inferior dental nerve
On the surface of the attached gingiva only
Into the floor of the mouth
Into one tooth's periodontal ligament
C.why: An intraligamentary injection goes into the periodontal ligament space beside a single tooth, using a special syringe.

whyNot.0: That describes an inferior dental block.
whyNot.2: The floor of the mouth isn't an LA injection site for teeth.

reteach.title: Think of a light switch
reteach.question: If each tooth were a light bulb, where would you flick the switch? At the bulb, or at the fuse box for the whole floor?

blocks.h: Bulb, fuse box, and the dimmer
blocks.body: An infiltration is like turning off one bulb: LA is placed near the tooth, and because upper jaw bone is thin, it soaks through to that tooth's nerve. A nerve block is the fuse box: inject near the main nerve and every tooth it supplies goes dark, along with the lip and chin. The vasoconstrictor is like a lid that keeps the LA where it was put, so the lights stay off longer. Too much LA reaching the bloodstream is a power surge through the whole house: that's toxicity.

explain.body: Topical gel numbs the surface. Infiltrations soak through thin bone, so they suit upper teeth and lower front teeth. The inferior dental block numbs all lower teeth on one side to the midline, plus the lip and chin. Intraligamentary injections numb a single tooth.

explain.caption: A right inferior dental block numbs the whole lower right quadrant, 41 to 48.

test.q: Which area does a right inferior dental block numb?
options: All the upper right teeth and gums
Both sides of the lower jaw
Only the lower right first molar
Lower right teeth, lip and chin
test.why: The block numbs the nerve supplying all the lower teeth on that side to the midline, plus the lower lip and chin (and often the tongue via the lingual nerve).

whyNot.0: Upper teeth are supplied by different nerves.
whyNot.1: A block works on one side only.
whyNot.2: A block numbs the whole quadrant, not one tooth.

explain.body: Lidocaine 2% with adrenaline 1:80,000 is the standard. Articaine 4% with adrenaline spreads well through bone. Prilocaine 3% with felypressin is used when adrenaline should be avoided, but not in pregnancy. Mepivacaine 3% is plain.

test.q: Which LA is generally avoided in pregnancy because of its vasoconstrictor?
options: Prilocaine 3% with felypressin
Lidocaine 2% with adrenaline
Articaine 4% with adrenaline
Mepivacaine 3% (no vasoconstrictor)
test.why: Felypressin is related to a hormone that can affect the uterus, so prilocaine with felypressin is generally avoided in pregnancy.

whyNot.1: Lidocaine with adrenaline is commonly regarded as suitable in pregnancy.

explain.body: Check the agent, expiry, cracks, clarity and the bung. Never resheath a needle by hand: use a safety syringe or resheathing device. The user disposes of the sharp into a yellow-lidded sharps bin.

test.q: Which bin should used LA cartridges go into?
options: Orange-lidded sharps bin
Black domestic waste
Yellow-lidded sharps bin
Tiger-stripe offensive bag
test.why: LA cartridges are medicinally contaminated sharps, so they go into the yellow-lidded sharps bin (HTM 07-01).

whyNot.0: Orange-lidded sharps bins are for sharps not contaminated with medicines.
whyNot.1: Sharps never go in domestic waste.
whyNot.3: Offensive waste bags must never contain sharps.

explain.body: Avoid eating and hot drinks until feeling returns; watch children. Fainting is the commonest problem. Toxicity shows as light-headedness, tingling around the mouth, ringing ears, slurred speech, twitching, then seizures and heart problems.

test.q: Which is the most common medical problem linked to dental injections?
options: Anaphylaxis
Cardiac arrest
Fainting
Severe toxicity
test.why: Fainting (vasovagal syncope), often from anxiety about the injection, is by far the most common.

whyNot.0: True allergy to modern dental LA is rare.
whyNot.3: Toxicity is uncommon at normal dental doses.
